items.title: Hallucination to Consensus: Multi-Agent LLMs for End-to-End JUnit Test Generation
items.abstract: Unit testing plays a critical role in ensuring software correctness. However, writing unit tests manually is labor-intensive, especially for strongly typed languages like Java, motivating the need for automated approaches. Traditional methods primarily rely on search-based or randomized algorithms to generate tests that achieve high code coverage and produce regression oracles, which are assertions derived from the program’s current behavior rather than its intended functionality. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled oracle generation from natural language descriptions, aligning better with user requirements. However, existing LLM-based methods often require LLM fine-tuning or rely on external tools such as EvoSuite for test prefix generation, making them costly or cumbersome to apply in practice. In this work, we propose CANDOR, a novel end-to-end, prompt engineering-based LLM framework for automated unit test generation in Java. CANDOR orchestrates multiple specialized LLM agents to collaboratively generate complete JUnit tests, including both high-quality test prefixes and accurate oracles. To mitigate the notorious hallucinations in LLMs and improve oracle correctness, we introduce a novel strategy that engages multiple reasoning LLMs in a panel discussion and generates accurate oracles based on consensus. Additionally, to reduce the verbosity of reasoning LLMs’ outputs, we propose a novel dual-LLM pipeline to produce concise and structured oracle evaluations. Our experiments on the HumanEvalJava and more complex LeetCodeJava datasets show that CANDOR is comparable with EvoSuite in generating tests with high code coverage and clearly superior in terms of mutation score. Moreover, our prompt engineering-based approach CANDOR significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art, fine-tuning-based oracle generator TOGLL by at least 21.1 percentage points in oracle correctness on both correct and faulty source code. Further ablation studies confirm the critical contributions of key agents in improving test prefix quality and oracle accuracy.

items.title: Handoff zones as the unit of analysis for AI accountability
items.abstract: Gap-based frameworks for AI accountability locate failure in static gaps: the responsibility gap, the liability gap, the accountability gap, the problem of many hands, the moral crumple zone, and Santoni de Sio and Mecacci’s four-part elaboration of the responsibility gap. Lifecycle approaches now emerging in policy literature extend accountability across a system’s evolution and value chain, including through monitoring, re-evaluation, and information sharing among actors. This paper asks a narrower question: whether, for the class of failures it takes as its object, the temporally extended relationship between actors should itself be treated as the primary unit of analysis. This paper develops the handoff zone as the appropriate primary unit of analysis for AI accountability failures characterized by temporal accumulation, asynchronous assumptions among actors, and recursive interdependence across a deployment chain. A handoff zone is the temporally extended envelope across which one actor transfers a system, a responsibility, or a set of expectations to another actor operating on asymmetric and evolving assumptions about the first. The framework draws on aviation human factors and patient safety literatures, where temporally extended handoff failures have been studied empirically for decades. Using Mobley v. Workday as its central case, supplemented by a hypothetical upstream provider transfer, the paper examines handoff relationships across the deployment chain and the downstream point at which their consequences reach applicants. Frameworks currently in use (risk-based classification, model documentation, audit, and lifecycle approaches) each do substantive analytical work; handoff-zone analysis makes the temporal envelope across which actors’ assumptions are renegotiated its primary object of analysis.

items.title: Happy 1000th Birthday, Kia Tūpato: Where Kia Tūpato Came From and Where It Is Heading
items.abstract: Legends and fairytales often centre on caution: Māui used a careful plan to slow the Sun, while Little Red Riding Hood sensed something was wrong with her grandmother. Kia Tūpato is a traditional Māori expression meaning caution. Rooted in Polynesian culture, it has moved through two key phases: its adoption by Māori and its continued use after European settlement. It is now entering a third phase as a digital workplace tool. This oral presentation traces the history of Kia Tūpato, presents findings from two recent case studies, and explores its use in workplaces and its emerging role as a digital app. The case studies show how Kia Tūpato can help workers make safer decisions, connect more effectively with workplace systems, and engage with decision-makers. Grounded in culture and practical relevance for Māori and many blue-collar workers, Kia Tūpato gives human factors and ergonomics practitioners a clear example of how cultural predispositions can shape worker decisions and support safer behaviour.

items.title: Helicopter accident patterns in Brazil from 2016 to 2025: analysis of consequences and recurrence
items.abstract: This study examines the most critical aeronautical occurrence scenarios involving helicopters in Brazil from 2016 to 2025, aiming to establish an exploratory framework to guide flight-safety mitigation strategies. Grounded in a quantitative approach utilizing official CENIPA data, the investigation incorporated Pareto diagrams and the Consequence and Recurrence Matrix (MCR). The findings identify Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) and Low Altitude Operation (LALT) as the most critical event types. Mechanical-failure categories (SCF-PP, SCF-NP) also demonstrated significant prevalence, suggesting a potential relationship with maintenance-related operational factors. In conclusion, addressing these operational risks demands a sociotechnical framework through robust Safety Management Systems (SMS) and the enhancement of CRM and MRM training protocols across both cockpit and hangar environments.

items.title: HeritageLens – AI-Powered Augmented Reality Heritage Guide
items.abstract: HeritageLens is an AI-powered Augmented Reality (AR) heritage guide designed to make exploring historical monuments more interactive and informative. Traditional methods of heritage exploration, such as information boards, printed materials and guided tours, often provide limited interaction and may not fully explain the historical importance of monuments. This paper presents HeritageLens, a system that combines Computer Vision-based monument recognition, historical information, AI-powered conversational assistance and location-based heritage discovery. It also explores features such as audio storytelling, multilingual explanations and AR-based visualisation to improve the overall learning experience. The application is designed to help tourists, students and heritage enthusiasts discover monuments, understand their historical significance and access information through a single platform. The paper discusses the system architecture, related research, development methodology, technologies used, evaluation framework and possible future improvements. The proposed system aims to make cultural heritage more accessible through the integration of Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision and Augmented Reality technologies.

items.title: Hi Gemini, Who Should I Vote For? The Benefits (and Problems) of Using LLMs As Voting Advice Applications
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores whether off-the-shelf LLMs could be used as voting advice applications (VAAs) to improve voter-party congruence. In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM’s advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM’s recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at ~1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM’s recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

items.title: Higher education at the core of research on generative artificial intelligence referring to Ecuador: a systematic mapping review (2024–2026)
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

items.title: How closely do large language model scores from parent interviews match self-reported parenting?
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear. We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents. Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving. Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency. Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model. Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction. Across parent–item pairs, 35.5%–44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents’ selected response categories. All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting. Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parent-reported scores. Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs. Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance. These findings support further evaluation of LLM-based parenting assessment while highlighting limitations in reproducing individual responses, matching score levels, and capturing some parenting dimensions.

items.title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
items.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

items.title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
items.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

items.title: Human-Centered Swarm Intelligence: Towards a Confucian Ideal of Great Harmony
items.abstract: To achieve his ideal of the Great Harmony (Datong), Confucius envisioned a society founded on the altruistic principle that “The world belongs to all”. Yet, inherent human self-interest has long rendered this vision utopian. The rise of the decentralized market economy in modern times has reframed the objective of resource allocation toward guiding self-interested individuals to achieve Pareto optimality—a state that resonates deeply with Confucius’ injunction: “Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.” Although the conditions for a fully functional decentralized market are highly demanding, advances in information technology and artificial intelligence are increasingly enabling us to approach them, thereby revitalizing the feasibility of a Datong society. However, a critical caveat remains: if general artificial intelligence evolves to serve only a minority rather than all equally, society could be driven in a direction diametrically opposed to the ideal of Great Harmony.

items.title: Human-computer interaction for recursive prompt and image generation on media narratives of violence in Mexico
items.abstract: Introduction This study explores media narratives of violence in Mexico through a hybrid human-computer interaction workflow combining computational analysis, human interpretation and generative artificial intelligence. Methods A non-probability corpus of 105 news items was analyzed to identify recurring terms, actors, locations and semantic relationships. Corpus summaries informed a workshop with 15 participants, who developed definitions and recursively refined text prompts and AI-generated images across five iterations. Textual and visual changes were analyzed, and experts supported their synthesis into an infographic and video. Results The selected corpus and workshop materials showed variation in textual and visual representations. Computational summaries made selected semantic differences explicit, while participants and experts supplied contextual interpretation. The process produced an infographic and video integrating these materials. Discussion The exploratory design does not estimate population parameters or establish causal effects. The workflow illustrates a human-led collaborative approach informed by mixed-initiative design: computational methods support structured comparison and generative variation, while people provide interpretation and critical judgment.

items.title: Human-in-the-Loop Available-to-Promise Intelligence for Reliable Delivery Date Prediction
items.abstract: Available-to-promise (ATP) systems increasingly rely on machine learning to predict delivery dates under conditions of fluctuating supply, capacity constraints, and demand variability. Yet purely algorithmic ATP pipelines face a persistent adoption barrier: planners and account teams frequently override or distrust automated delivery-date predictions, particularly after observing even isolated forecasting errors, a pattern long documented in the algorithm-aversion literature. Conversely, human-only override regimes reintroduce the inconsistency and latency that automation was meant to eliminate. This paper proposes a human-in-the-loop (HITL) available-to-promise intelligence framework that resolves this tension by design rather than by policy. Following a design science research approach, the framework separates delivery-date prediction into four architectural layers: an algorithmic prediction layer, a confidence and uncertainty estimation layer, a human-review trigger layer governed by explicit escalation criteria, and an override/feedback-capture layer that closes the loop back into model governance. The trigger layer operationalises when a prediction should reach a human reviewer, using confidence thresholds, anomalous order-pattern detection, and value/risk tiering rather than blanket human review or blanket automation. The paper situates this design against literature on algorithm aversion and appreciation, human-in-the-loop machine learning architectures, and explainability in supply-chain artificial intelligence and evaluates the framework's utility against design science research criteria rather than primary empirical validation. The paper closes with an explicit limitations discussion and a concrete agenda for the multi-case empirical validation the framework's real-world deployment would require.

items.title: Human-LLM Cognitive Extension: A Framework for Studying Coupled Cognition
items.abstract: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

items.abstract: Human–AI Charter Public Consultation: 14 Key Questions on Governability, Risk Control and Room to Develop This discussion paper invites public comment on the Human–AI Charter (Public Consultation Draft). Its central idea is to govern how AI capabilities are translated into real-world power, not intelligence itself. AI may learn, reason and research freely; but when it gains the ability to move money, operate equipment, touch infrastructure or decide on someone's behalf, that power must have a lawful source and clear limits, and stay provable, reviewable and open to remedy. The paper sets out 14 open questions in four groups: governability (G1–G4), risk control (R1–R4), room to develop (D1–D3), and legitimacy and the future (L1–L3). It also includes two candidate new clauses for consultation, not yet part of the charter text: (A) responsibility registers for high-risk AI, and (B) an independent public forum for users as a "fourth estate" of AI governance. This consultation remains open, with no closing date. Please send comments, quoting the question number (e.g. G2, R3), to humanaicharter@gmail.com. items.title: Illocutionary Explanation Planning for Source-Faithful Explanations in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
items.abstract: Natural language explanations produced by large language models (LLMs) are often persuasive, but not necessarily scrutable: users cannot easily verify whether the claims in an explanation are supported by evidence. In XAI, this motivates a focus on faithfulness and traceability, i.e., the extent to which an explanation’s claims can be grounded in, and traced back to, an explicit source. We study these desiderata in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for programming education, where textbooks provide authoritative evidence. We benchmark six LLMs on 90 Stack Overflow questions grounded in three programming textbooks and quantify source faithfulness via source adherence metrics. We find that non Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have median source adherence of 0%, while baseline RAG systems still exhibit low median adherence (22–40%, depending on the model). Motivated by Achinstein’s illocutionary theory of explanation, we introduce illocutionary macro-planning as a descriptive design principle for source-faithful explanations and instantiate it with chain-of-illocution prompting (CoI), which expands a query into implicit explanatory questions that drive retrieval. Across models, CoI yields statistically significant gains (up to 63%) in source adherence, although absolute adherence remains moderate and the gains are weak or non-significant for some models. A user study with 165 retained participants (220 recruited) indicates that these gains do not harm satisfaction, relevance, or perceived correctness. Data and Code: https://github.com/Francesco-Sovrano/chain-of-illocution

items.title: Improving AI-assisted grading reliability through explicit rubric and prompt engineering
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment and feedback in higher education has attracted growing interest, but concerns remain about the consistency and appropriateness of AI-generated grades in summative contexts. This study examined whether a combined calibration strategy involving a more explicit rubric and marking prompt could improve agreement between AI-assisted grading and educator judgement in a laboratory-based STEM assessment. We compared educator-assigned marks for 40 graduate Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems laboratory reports with marks generated by GPT-5 under pre- and post-calibration configurations, and examined agreement using complementary statistical and visual analyses. Following calibration, agreement with educator marks improved across measures of score correspondence and absolute agreement: the intraclass correlation coefficient increased from 0.818 to 0.928, the mean AI-educator difference decreased from +1.625 to +1.041 marks, and no post-calibration report differed from the educator mark by more than 10 marks. These findings suggest that the way assessment criteria, evidence requirements, and marking rules are specified can materially influence AI-human grading agreement. However, the revised rubric and prompt were introduced together, calibration drew on discrepancies observed in the same 40 reports used for post-calibration evaluation, and one educator's marks served as the reference. The results therefore support improved in-sample agreement under a human-supervised calibration strategy, rather than establishing grading validity or interchangeability for autonomous summative decisions.

items.title: Improving predictive accuracy for clinical outcomes with LLM text embeddings for open-ended free-text responses: A case study on reports of psychedelic experiences
items.abstract: Clinical studies regularly ask participants to describe their experiences in their own words. These open-ended questions are included so that participants can report what they themselves consider relevant, and ideally researchers want to harvest this information. In practice however, these responses are rarely analyzed and often effectively discarded, since translating them into a useful quantitative format for further analysis traditionally required trained coders or advanced technical skills. Current transformer-based language models offer an appealing alternative option to quantify text: they internally represent any text input as high-dimensional numerical representations called text embeddings. Fromavailable open-weight models, these text embeddings can be freely extracted on a local machine. As text embeddings are just vectors of numbers, they can be plugged as predictors into standard statistical analyses. Here, we applied this to three large datasets in which participants described their experiences in the context of psychedelic substance use. We investigated whether text embeddings of these free-text descriptions improve cross-validated, held-out predictions of clinically relevant outcomes (well-being, change in well-being, change in psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity, post-traumatic growth) after we control for a range of other predictors capturingdemographic information, the setting of the experience, and a series of questionnaire data. We found reliable increases in predictive accuracy for three of the five outcomes (change in well-being and psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity), in two of the three datasets. Some of these increases are substantial. We therefore recommend (where possible) the inclusion of open-ended questions in any questionnaire, and to actually pass this information to analysis, to efficiently capture valuable information that would otherwise be lost.

items.title: Incremental Speciation in Evolutionary Red Teaming of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Speciation maintains distinct subpopulations in evolutionary search through similarity-based grouping and species-aware parent selection. For text-based individuals, niches depend on both the compatibility representation and the assignment operator that turns pairwise relations into species. We examine this design space in black-box evolutionary red teaming of large language models, comparing embedding and natural language inference (NLI) dissimilarities under representative-based and density-based speciation. Offline calibration on a 3,139-prompt archive shows that MiniLM embedding dissimilarity ($d_E$) and DeBERTa-v3-small NLI non-entailment ($d_{\neg E}$) produce different species structures at the same nominal threshold. Even with pairwise edge density matched to MiniLM, NLI density connectivity forms a few concentrated, mixed-topic species, with substantially more off-topic membership. These structural differences persist online under a matched evaluation budget. The endpoint top-50 median fitness favors incremental DBSCAN over leader-follower, but bootstrap intervals from 10 runs include zero, providing no reliable evidence of an advantage. Semantic diversity among top prompts declines in every configuration, with no consistent method advantage. The clearest difference concerns high-fitness population occupancy: MiniLM incremental DBSCAN maintains mature niches across seed topics, whereas NLI incremental DBSCAN attains the same highest observed median fitness while concentrating high-fitness prompts in variants of a few seed topics. Thus, representation-dependent connectivity predicts population structure more consistently than endpoint fitness. Species count alone does not establish quality-diversity, and more species do not necessarily preserve semantically diverse high-fitness prompts.

items.title: Independent Research Essays on AI, Society, Power, and Structural Change: A Collection of Fifteen Analytical Works
items.abstract: DESCRIPTION This collection brings together fifteen independently authored research essays and analytical works examining artificial intelligence, social structures, political authority, economic inequality, cybersecurity, digital identity, institutional accountability, and the changing relationship between individuals and complex technological systems. Originally published as individual works through Substack, these essays approach contemporary technological and social transformations from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Some investigate technical and epistemic limitations in AI systems, cybersecurity, information infrastructure, and digital continuity. Others examine political polarization, religious authority, generational inheritance, labor-market exclusion, economic stratification, institutional recognition, and the distribution of power. Several works also explore questions concerning the reconstruction of personal identity through informational systems, the relationship between memory and continuity, and the consequences of transferring human judgment or authority into increasingly autonomous technological environments. The collection does not advance a single unified theory or claim that all included works share the same methodology. Instead, it documents an evolving independent research program organized around several recurring questions: What happens when the systems used to observe reality become incapable of representing the conditions that actually exist? How do institutions, political structures, and economic arrangements determine who receives opportunities, recognition, and the benefits of collective contribution? How are memory, identity, authority, and inherited social structures transformed when technological systems begin to mediate increasingly fundamental aspects of human life? Why do institutions repeatedly struggle to address structural vulnerabilities even when their underlying causes are already identifiable? And what forms of accountability, institutional adaptation, and technical architecture are necessary when existing systems can no longer reliably manage the complexity they have created? The works included here range from technical proposals and systems analysis to political and socioeconomic commentary, conceptual frameworks, and exploratory scenarios. Their evidentiary foundations and analytical methods therefore vary according to their respective subjects. Together, they examine a recurring structural problem: the growing distance between what complex systems represent, what institutions reward, what individuals experience, and what society is actually capable of verifying. This collection should be understood as an archival record of independent research and analysis rather than a unified theoretical framework. Its individual publications retain their respective arguments, assumptions, methodological boundaries, and limitations. CONTENTS 01. items.title: Industrial Internet of Agents: Conceptual Architecture, Applications, and Challenges
items.abstract: AI agents driven by foundation models have shown potential for industrial automation beyond rule-based control. However, existing studies differ in how industrial agents collaborate and how their systems are tested, making it difficult to compare networking requirements and physical execution capabilities. This paper examines the intersection of networked agents and industrial automation, where industrial signals, communication constraints, contextual information, and operational requirements must be considered jointly. It develops the Industrial Internet of Agents (IIoA) and presents a conceptual architecture for analyzing industrial deployment requirements. Building on the Internet of Agents (IoA) framework, IIoA re-specifies sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution through eleven industrial extensions. Representative studies are synthesized across shopfloor operations, autonomous plant operations and maintenance, supply chain collaboration, and digital twin systems. The analysis indicates that industrial agent networking requires the joint design of semantic coordination, operational technology (OT) interoperability, latency-aware deployment, trust governance, and verifiable physical execution. Finally, seven open challenges are identified, covering reliability, latency, protocol integrity, scalability, physical grounding, adaptability, and evaluation.

items.title: Inferential Disclosure Through Joined Fragments: How Separate Pieces Can Say What None of Them Said
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Inferential Disclosure Through Joined Fragments, a mechanism by which separately disclosed pieces of information become available to one reader, who can connect them to infer a relationship that no piece established alone. The paper asks how strongly the evidence supports the connection and whether the purposes for which the fragments were disclosed permit their combined use. A reader may have strong grounds for an identification while permission to make that use of the records remains unsettled. The first case concerns the Japanese designator “AF” before the Battle of Midway. By March 1942, analysts at Corregidor had identified AF as Midway, while disagreement persisted in Washington. In May, Midway sent an uncoded message reporting a shortage of fresh water. A subsequent Japanese report attributed a water shortage to AF. The shared detail connected the two messages and corroborated the earlier identification. The second case concerns AOL’s 2006 release of search queries grouped under user numbers. One number brought together searches mentioning a town, a surname, and a housing subdivision. Reporters followed those clues to Thelma Arnold, who recognized the searches as her own. She explained that she had researched some symptoms for friends. The evidence supported identifying who had conducted the searches while leaving open whom any particular search described. The paper places this case alongside Latanya Sweeney’s work on re-identification through linked records. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. A draft exhibition program might list a title and booking code, while a venue’s schedule lists the same code and a room. An AI assistant could infer where the exhibition is planned. Whether the organizers authorized combining those records for a public announcement is a separate question.

items.title: Inquiry-Induced Depletion of Later Examination Capacity: How a Check Can Use Up What Later Checks Need
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Inquiry-Induced Depletion of Later Examination Capacity, an account of how one inquiry can consume a resource that a later inquiry also needs. The resource may be material, time, attention, or cooperation. A check can answer its immediate question accurately and still leave a later question harder to examine. The cost depends on what that later question requires and how much of the resource remains available to answer it. The paper sets out three requirements for identifying depletion. An assessment must name the shared resource, establish what the earlier inquiry consumed, and identify a later question whose examination depended on what was lost. This requires comparing what was available before and after the inquiry and considering other causes of the loss. A record may preserve enough evidence for a particular later question, attention may recover, and learning from the first inquiry may offset some of its cost. The paper places the mechanism alongside the 1992 Valletta Convention’s provision for archaeological reserves and examines two documented cases. Near Xi’an, excavation exposed the painted terracotta figures of the First Emperor of Qin. Once exposed, the lacquer beneath the pigment could flake away within minutes, taking with it evidence of the figures’ original colors. Apollo 17 sample 73001 illustrates preservation. NASA kept the lunar sample sealed for nearly 50 years. In 2022, researchers used X-ray computed tomography to record the core’s internal arrangement before removing and dividing it for study. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can sequence or stop an examination and who bears the cost when a shared resource runs low. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is the allocation of reviewer time. If an AI assistant requests several routine checks before a deadline, an evaluator could trace how much time those checks consumed and whether the reviewer still had enough time to examine a disputed source on which the final judgment depended.

items.title: Institutional Crutches: The Ba Sing Se Doctrine
items.abstract: Modern sociotechnical systems—spanning sovereign signals intelligence, hyperscale semiconductor supply chains, connected automotive infrastructure, and frontier artificial intelligence laboratories—exhibit a recurring divergence between physical system state (C) and institutional representation (I). When architectural shortcuts, default-open perimeters, or circular capital commitments generate structural failures, governing bodies rarely initiate immediate remediation. Instead, they execute a standardized crisis-containment protocol termed The Ba Sing Se Doctrine: an active administrative posture that suppresses internal error signals until an external leak forces public visibility, at which point the institution issues formal decrees reclassifying systemic breaches as routine maintenance, isolated personal errors, or resolved minor friction. Tracing this mechanism from classical imperial theater at the Hellespont and the English Channel to four concurrent November 2026 infrastructure and technology crises, this paper formalizes the structural anatomy of zero-admission governance and demonstrates why narrative equilibrium accelerates physical collapse.

items.title: Integrating Without Conflating: A Safety-Culture-Anchored Conceptual Review of Construct Boundaries from Safety Climate to Worker Well-Being
items.abstract: Safety culture, psychosocial safety, work design and worker well-being are increasingly considered together, although they describe different organisational conditions, processes and outcomes. We conducted a safety-culture-anchored conceptual review informed by structured bibliographic searching and purposive source selection to examine these boundaries. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science on 29 June 2026 identified 3129 records. A dated duplicate audit reconciled 2500 report records; 28 verified complete texts from a 44-source conceptual set supported detailed synthesis. Recurrent organisational practices concerned management commitment, enacted priorities, resources, communication, participation, justice and feedback for improvement. Their recurrence did not establish a single higher-order construct. The synthesis compares referents, levels, mechanisms, measurement and outcomes across safety, psychosocial-health and well-being approaches. It provides explicit rules for connecting these entities without treating their measures or outcomes as interchangeable. Three conditional propositions specify future tests of construct discrimination, cross-domain pathways and diagnostic usefulness. Purposive selection, incomplete records of later selection decisions, unequal coverage of adjacent fields and the absence of documented independent duplicate screening limit coverage and reproducibility. The proposed framework is a conceptual interpretation, not a validated causal model.
